title: Harvey Power Users: The 'Aha!' Moment — Chanley Howell and Kelly Boyd at Foley & Lardner
author: Harvey Team · Chanley Howell · Kelly Boyd

dom.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source summary contains only content titles and no substantive claims, evidence, reasoning or quotations. Its position on selective deployment, verification and work redesign therefore cannot be determined.

st.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value
st.an: The source directly supports the proposition that licences and usage alone do not create organisational value. It links effective adoption to sustained training, peer support and movement from experimentation into value-producing practice, while treating human review as necessary. Its efficiency and quality claims are task-level self-reports, not evidence of firm-wide outcomes.
qs: But it’s important to note that buying the license is just the first step — then you've got to do all this work to build adoption.

Together, the team is on a mission to increase training resources, expand support, and build out peer teams so we can help more people reach that “aha!” moment, while also giving power users like us the structure to move from experimentation to delivering real value.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s qualified account of positive but interested and anecdotal operational evidence. It provides a concrete example of near-client-ready output and identifies power users driving wider adoption, but offers no systematic performance evidence or basis for inferring durable defensibility.
qs: One time I put a transcript of a client call into Harvey with a little context, and it gave me almost client-ready advice.
We've been the two most active users with Harvey.

kp.k: Power users report substantial task-specific time savings
kp.d: In this Harvey company-blog interview, Foley & Lardner attorneys Kelly Boyd and Chanley Howell report personal experience rather than measured firm-wide results. Boyd says certain tasks fell from five hours to one, also describing this as roughly 25% of the original time; those figures are not equivalent. Howell estimates that reviewing and marking up technology, software and cloud agreements takes 25 to 30% of the previous time from start to finish.
qs: I have found certain tasks that would have taken me five hours now take me one. So roughly 25% of the time.
For reviewing and marking up some agreements — something we do every day with technology, software, and cloud agreements — it probably takes 25 to 30% of the time from start to finish.

kp.k: Reported benefits include better analysis, not just speed
kp.d: Howell claims that AI-assisted work product is often better and that saved time can be used to strengthen analysis and add insights. He highlights thoroughness in contract review and compliance issue spotting, and recounts one instance in which Harvey generated almost client-ready advice from a client-call transcript and context. These are practitioner assessments and an individual example, not comparative quality measurements.
qs: And the work product often is better. We can then use that time to tighten our analysis and provide additional insights.
We always talk about quicker, but there's a lot of better to it also, the thoroughness of it in reviewing contracts or spotting compliance issues.
One time I put a transcript of a client call into Harvey with a little context, and it gave me almost client-ready advice.

kp.k: System-generated drafts still require thorough human verification
kp.d: Boyd describes receiving initial drafts from a system instead of a person, while retaining thorough review before client delivery. Howell similarly frames Harvey as a tool that neither performs the lawyer's entire job nor guarantees complete accuracy. Their account describes assisted legal work with human verification, rather than autonomous client-ready delivery.
qs: Instead of getting initial drafts from a person, you're getting it from a system. But just like any work, it needs to be thoroughly reviewed prior to having a client-ready version.
The second most important thing is to be open-minded and flexible, and recognize it's a tool.
It's not going to do your job or do everything 100% accurately for you, but it will absolutely allow you to do things quicker and better.

kp.k: Distributed law-firm structures make adoption an organisational challenge
kp.d: Boyd argues that partners' relatively autonomous practices mean adoption depends on individuals recognising value and actually using the technology. Buying licences is only the first step. She reports that Foley & Lardner established an AI Steering Committee and hired AI Director Sean Monahan, with plans to increase training, expand support and build peer teams for both new adopters and experienced users.
qs: Law firms are very distributed, every partner has their own mini-business. You're dependent on people understanding the value and using it.
But it’s important to note that buying the license is just the first step — then you've got to do all this work to build adoption.
Our management team put in place an AI Steering Committee and hired an AI Director, Sean Monahan, to help lead the charge.

Together, the team is on a mission to increase training resources, expand support, and build out peer teams so we can help more people reach that “aha!” moment, while also giving power users like us the structure to move from experimentation to delivering real value.

kp.k: Power-user development requires sustained learning and openness
kp.d: Howell recommends substantial investment in training alongside flexibility and openness. Boyd reports attending Harvey training almost every week and continuing to learn despite avid use since licence activation. Both identify personal receptiveness to technology and opportunity as factors in adoption, while Boyd explicitly couples opportunity with understanding risks and responsible use.
qs: You're going to need to invest a lot of time learning and training — that's number one.
I go to the Harvey training sessions almost every week now, and every single time I still learn something.
Part of it is personality. Where some people see mostly risk, others see opportunity.

While Chanley and I definitely understood the risks from day one, we also saw immediately where things were inevitably headed and that understanding the tools and the responsible use of the tools would be the way to unlock the opportunity.

kp.k: Visible practical benefits are expected to spread peer adoption
kp.d: Howell identifies a breakthrough moment when benefits become clear as important to becoming a power user. Boyd proposes a peer-diffusion mechanism: users who experience that moment tell colleagues, who then recruit others. This is their explanation of how adoption can build, not a quantified finding about uptake.
qs: But you also need to reach that "aha!" moment where the benefits become clear.
The key is getting people to that "aha!" moment, where they tell two friends, and then those two tell two friends, and so on and so on. And then it starts really building.

kp.k: Boyd anticipates profession-wide disruption comparable to industrial revolution
kp.d: Boyd characterises legal AI as the beginning of what she believes is a second Industrial Revolution for the profession, with unusually large opportunities. This is her broad interpretation and expectation of technological disruption, rather than evidence of specific changes to employment, pricing or market structure.
qs: When I first saw Harvey, I saw immediately that we were at the start of what I believe to be the equivalent of a second Industrial Revolution hitting our profession in a way that perhaps other disruptive technologies have not.
It's like a bomb dropped in the middle of the legal profession, and anytime you have disruptive technology like that, the opportunity is incredible.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Boyd and Howell report substantial time savings on selected tasks, with Howell also claiming improvements in work quality.
pts.d: Kelly Boyd reports that certain tasks previously taking five hours now take one, which she describes as roughly 25% of the previous time; the five-to-one example itself implies 20%. Chanley Howell reports that reviewing and marking up some technology, software and cloud agreements takes 25–30% of the previous time from start to finish. Howell says the work product is often better and that saved time can be used to refine analysis and add insights. These are task-specific accounts, not estimates of firm-wide productivity.

pts.k: Howell and Boyd describe AI as augmenting lawyers and changing the source of initial drafts, rather than autonomously delivering finished legal work.
pts.d: Howell claims that Harvey enables quicker and better work, including more thorough contract review and compliance issue spotting. He recounts a client-call transcript producing almost client-ready advice after he supplied context. Boyd describes obtaining initial drafts from a system instead of a person, while retaining thorough human verification before client delivery. Neither speaker claims that the tool can replace the lawyer's entire job.

pts.k: Boyd presents AI as a potentially profession-transforming disruption; both speakers say realising its benefits requires active adoption work.
pts.d: Boyd characterises the profession as being at the start of a second Industrial Revolution, expressing a broad expectation rather than a quantified market forecast. She argues that licence purchases alone do not deliver adoption in a decentralised law firm. Howell stresses training, flexibility and experiencing a clear benefit. Boyd predicts that such breakthrough experiences can spread use through peer recommendations. She reports that Foley & Lardner has established an AI Steering Committee and hired an AI Director, with plans to increase training, support and peer teams; these are reported organisational actions and intentions, not measured outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists of two active users' first-person experiences and organisational accounts, published in Harvey's company blog.
pts.d: The May 18, 2026 interview identifies Howell and Boyd as among Foley & Lardner's most active Harvey users. Their support includes retrospective task-duration estimates, subjective assessments of work quality, a single transcript-to-advice example, and Boyd's experience of ongoing training. No timing study, sample size, independent quality assessment, benchmark or firm-wide outcome data is supplied. Boyd's profession-wide transformation prediction and peer-diffusion account are presented as beliefs and practical expectations, rather than empirically established forecasts. The blog links to a broader RSGI feature but does not reproduce its evidence.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Productivity benefits are described as already occurring by the interview's publication; broader transformation and adoption expansion have no specified completion date.
pts.d: The source was published on May 18, 2026. Task savings and drafting benefits are current or retrospective experiences, confined to certain tasks and some agreements. The speakers condition effective use on substantial learning, openness, responsible use and human verification, explicitly rejecting expectations of perfect accuracy or complete job automation. Firm support is being formalised at the time of the interview. Boyd's Industrial Revolution analogy implies an early stage of longer-term change, without a numerical forecast or deadline.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The concrete effects concern lawyers and adoption leaders at Foley & Lardner, with potential benefits to their clients; the broader profession is the subject of Boyd's transformation prediction.
pts.d: Howell, identified as a partner, and Boyd, identified as of counsel, report changes to their own workflows. Technology, software and cloud agreement work is the clearest practice-specific example. Other firm attorneys are intended beneficiaries of expanded training and peer support, while management, the AI Steering Committee and AI Director organise adoption. Clients may receive tighter analysis, additional insights and reviewed AI-assisted work, but the source does not report lower client fees or measured client outcomes. Although Boyd describes systems supplying drafts previously obtained from people, the source does not identify a displaced staffing group or predict headcount reductions.
